sub_units.name: Basic Array Traversal & Operations
sub_units.content:
Arrays are one of the most fundamental and widely used data structures in computer science. An array is a linear data structure that stores multiple elements of the same data type in contiguous memory locations. Because the elements are stored continuously in memory, arrays provide fast and efficient access to data.

Each element inside an array is identified using an index. Indexing starts from 0 because the index represents the offset from the starting memory address. For example:

["Song A", "Song B", "Song C"]

• Song A → Index 0  
• Song B → Index 1  
• Song C → Index 2  

Arrays support several important operations such as traversal, access, update, insertion, and deletion.

Array traversal means visiting each element one by one to perform operations like printing values, calculating sums, finding maximum values, or updating elements. Traversal can happen in two ways:

1. Forward Traversal  
Elements are visited from beginning to end.

2. Backward Traversal  
Elements are visited from end to beginning.

Arrays provide Random Access, meaning any element can be directly accessed using its index without traversing previous elements. This operation takes O(1) time complexity.

For example:
numbers[2]

directly accesses the third element.

Update operation means replacing an existing element with a new value. Since the position is already known, update operations also take O(1) time.

Insertion and deletion operations depend on position:

• Insertion at the end is usually fast.  
• Insertion at the beginning or middle requires shifting elements to the right.  
• Deletion from the middle requires shifting elements to the left.  

Because of shifting, insertion and deletion in the middle generally take O(n) time complexity.

Real-Life Example:
A music playlist is a simple real-world example of arrays. Songs are stored one after another, and users can directly access any song using its position in the playlist.

sub_units.name: Searching in Arrays
sub_units.content:
Searching in arrays means finding the position or index of a specific element inside an array. Searching is one of the most important operations because many applications require locating data quickly and efficiently.

The most basic searching technique is Linear Search.

In Linear Search:
• Elements are checked one by one from beginning to end.  
• The search continues until the target element is found.  
• If the element is not found, the algorithm returns -1.

Example:
Array = [10, 20, 30, 40]  
Target = 30

The algorithm checks:
• 10 → not match  
• 20 → not match  
• 30 → match found  

Output:
2

Linear Search has a time complexity of O(n) because in the worst case every element may need to be checked.

Arrays also support direct element access using indexes because memory addresses are calculated mathematically using:

Address(i) = Base + (i × Size)

Where:
• Base = starting memory address  
• i = index  
• Size = size of each element  

This direct calculation helps arrays achieve fast random access.

Real-Life Examples:
• Searching for a student name in an attendance sheet  
• Finding a song in a playlist  
• Searching for a contact number in a contact list  
• Locating records in a database  

Searching operations are very important in software development because efficient searching improves overall application performance.

sub_units.name: Array Rearrangement
sub_units.content:
Array rearrangement refers to changing the order or position of elements inside an array based on certain conditions. Rearrangement techniques are widely used in problem solving, optimization, and data organization.

Common rearrangement operations include:
• Reversing arrays  
• Shifting elements  
• Moving zeros to the end  
• Swapping elements  
• Inserting elements at specific positions  
• Deleting elements  

Insertion Operation:
When an element is inserted in the middle or beginning of an array, existing elements must shift one position to the right.

Example:
Before insertion:
[A] [B] [C] [D]

Insert X at index 1:
[A] [X] [B] [C] [D]

This shifting process takes O(n) time complexity.

Deletion Operation:
When an element is deleted from the middle, remaining elements shift left to fill the empty space.

Example:
Before deletion:
[A] [B] [C] [D]

Delete B:
[A] [C] [D]

Deletion from the middle also takes O(n) time complexity.

Array reversing is another common rearrangement problem where elements from both ends are swapped repeatedly until the array is reversed.

Real-Life Examples:
• Rearranging books on a shelf  
• Adjusting students in a classroom row  
• Organizing songs in a playlist  
• Sorting products in an online store  

Rearrangement problems help improve logical thinking and strengthen understanding of in-place array manipulation techniques.

sub_units.name: Subarray Problems
sub_units.content:
A subarray is a contiguous portion of an array. Subarray problems are extremely important in data structures and algorithms because many real-world problems involve working with continuous segments of data.

Example:
Array = [1, 2, 3, 4]

Possible subarrays:
[1]
[1,2]
[2,3]
[2,3,4]

Subarray problems commonly involve:
• Finding maximum sum subarray  
• Finding minimum sum subarray  
• Range sum queries  
• Fixed-size window calculations  
• Continuous segment optimization  

One of the most important concepts used in subarray problems is the Prefix Sum Array.

A Prefix Sum Array stores cumulative sums.

Formula:
prefix[i] = prefix[i−1] + arr[i]

Example:
Original array:
[2, 3, 4, 5]

Prefix sum array:
[2, 5, 9, 14]

Using prefix sums, range sums can be calculated efficiently using:

Sum(L,R) = prefix[R] − prefix[L−1]

This avoids repeated addition and improves performance significantly.

Real-Life Example:
Suppose a bank records daily deposits:
[100, 200, 300, 400]

If the manager wants the total deposits from Day 2 to Day 4, prefix sums allow the result to be calculated instantly without repeatedly adding values.

Subarray concepts are widely used in:
• Financial systems  
• Data analytics  
• Competitive programming  
• Signal processing  
• Performance optimization problems

sub_units.name: Two Pointer / Sliding Window
sub_units.content:
The Two Pointer and Sliding Window techniques are advanced optimization approaches used to solve array and string problems efficiently. These methods help reduce unnecessary computations and improve time complexity.

Two Pointer Technique:
The two pointer approach uses two indexes that move through the array simultaneously.

It is commonly used for:
• Reversing arrays  
• Pair sum problems  
• Sorted array problems  
• Removing duplicates  
• Comparing elements from both ends  

Example:
To reverse an array:
• One pointer starts from the beginning  
• Another pointer starts from the end  
• Elements are swapped while pointers move toward each other  

This approach improves efficiency and reduces extra memory usage.

Sliding Window Technique:
Sliding window is used for problems involving continuous subarrays or ranges.

Instead of recalculating values repeatedly:
• A window of elements is maintained  
• Elements are added and removed dynamically  
• Calculations are updated efficiently  

This technique is very useful for:
• Maximum sum subarray problems  
• Fixed-size subarray problems  
• Longest substring problems  
• Continuous segment analysis  

Advantages:
• Reduces unnecessary traversal  
• Improves performance  
• Optimizes repeated calculations  
• Useful for large datasets  

Real-Life Examples:
• Monitoring temperature changes over consecutive days  
• Calculating moving averages in finance  
• Analyzing continuous user activity in applications  
• Processing streaming data efficiently  

These techniques are widely used in competitive programming, interviews, and real-world software systems because they provide highly optimized solutions.

questions.title: Sort an Array of 0s, 1s, and 2s
questions.content:
Given an array containing only 0s, 1s, and 2s, sort it in-place without using any built-in sort function. The relative order of equal elements does not matter.

This is also known as the **Dutch National Flag Problem**.

**Constraints:**
- 1 <= n <= 10^5
- arr[i] ∈ {0, 1, 2}
questions.inputFormat:
First line: integer n (size of array).
Second line: n space-separated integers (0, 1, or 2).
questions.outputFormat: A single line with n space-separated integers in sorted order.

examples.explanation: Dutch flag: move 0s to left, 2s to right, 1s in middle.
After sorting: all 0s, then 1s, then 2s.

hints: Use three pointers: low (left boundary for 0s), mid (current element), high (right boundary for 2s).
If arr[mid]=0 swap with arr[low] and advance both low and mid. If arr[mid]=2 swap with arr[high] and decrease high. If arr[mid]=1 just advance mid.
The algorithm runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space — a single pass through the array.

import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0]); arr = list(map(int, data[1:n+1]))
lo, mid, hi = 0, 0, n - 1
while mid <= hi:
    if arr[mid] == 0: arr[lo], arr[mid] = arr[mid], arr[lo]; lo += 1; mid += 1
    elif arr[mid] == 2: arr[mid], arr[hi] = arr[hi], arr[mid]; hi -= 1
    else: mid += 1
print(' '.join(map(str, arr)))
